blocks.content: A canary deployment sends a small percentage of real traffic to a new version first, watching it closely before gradually increasing that percentage, a meaningfully lower-risk approach than blue-green's all-at-once cutover.

Rather than cutting over completely, a canary deployment routes only a small slice of real traffic, perhaps 5%, to the new version, while the vast majority continues hitting the proven, existing version.

blocks.alt: A small, deliberate slice of real traffic, not an all-or-nothing switch

blocks.content: The entire point is observation, error rates, latency, and other real metrics from that small slice are watched closely, only once the new version proves itself does the percentage increase further, step by step.

blocks.alt: Real observation gating every further step, not a blind, scheduled rollout

blocks.content: Within plain Kubernetes primitives alone, canary can be approximated crudely, two Deployments (old and new) behind the same Service selector, with deliberately uneven replica counts, roughly approximating a percentage split, since Service load balancing distributes evenly across matching Pods.

blocks.alt: An approximate split, achieved through nothing more than uneven replica counts

blocks.content:

# Both share the same Service selector, roughly a 90/10 split

blocks.content: For a genuinely precise percentage split, rather than the rough approximation above, you need real traffic-splitting capability, either through Ingress annotations supporting canary routing, or a full service mesh, covered in the Service Mesh category, giving fine-grained, accurate control over exactly what percentage goes where.

blocks.alt: Real precision requires dedicated traffic-splitting tooling, not just replica counts

blocks.content: Canary's core advantage over blue-green is limiting the blast radius of a problem, if the new version has a real issue, only that small percentage of users were ever affected, compared to blue-green's all-or-nothing exposure the moment the switch happens.

blocks.alt: A meaningfully smaller blast radius if something turns out to be wrong

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Canary sends a small percentage of traffic to a new version first, gradually increasing it based on real observed metrics, not a native Kubernetes feature either.
A crude version is achievable with uneven replica counts, a precise one needs real traffic-splitting via Ingress or a service mesh, and it genuinely limits blast radius versus blue-green.
